Turbine inlet gas temperatures in advanced aircraft engines can reach 2500°F (1371°C) and above.
Turbine inlet pressures in advanced engines can reach 25 to 30 atmospheres, with future plans for 40 atmospheres.
Current 2D boundary layer analysis programs can have errors up to 35% in predicting heat transfer coefficients on the suction side of turbine blades.
A 100°F (55.5°C) error in predicted blade surface temperature can reduce the estimated blade life by an order of magnitude.
Stagnation region Nusselt numbers are directly proportional to the square root of the Reynolds number, with a proportionality constant sensitive to upstream turbulence level.
Increased upstream turbulence can amplify turbulence levels near the stagnation region, enhancing local heat transfer by up to 19%.
Analytical models have struggled to accurately predict the level of heat transfer augmentation due to upstream turbulence effects.
The flow through a turbine blade row is highly complex, involving stagnation, curvature effects, acceleration, secondary flows, and transition/detransition processes.
Unsteadiness in the flow entering the turbine, due to the compressor and combustion processes, can significantly impact the heat transfer.
Three different definitions have been proposed to quantify flow unsteadiness: overall disturbance level, free-stream turbulence level, and unsteadiness level.
